source.title: Hierarchical Latent Structures in Data Generation Process Unify Mechanistic Phenomena across Scale
source.authors: Jonas Rohweder; Subhabrata Dutta; Iryna Gurevych

page_placements.theme: What sets the amount of compensation: training data, objective, pretraining stage, width/scale, training under a lesion

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study ablates layer outputs and measures changes in downstream predictive influence, directly testing layer-level compensation on new synthetic models and an OLMo checkpoint.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses induction heads, function vectors, copy suppression, and other mechanisms, but those are not results about the claim versions unless they directly measure layerwise or headwise compensation. The headwise experiment measures a target-token predictive-influence score, not compensation on the full output distribution.
record.test_reason: The study zeroes a layer's output and measures the change in later layers' direct target-token logit contribution. That is close to McGrath et al.'s direct-effect compensation measure. It applies this to toy models, 17M models trained on PCSG or N-gram data, and OLMo-1B checkpoints, so its results bear on V1. The headwise results come from synthetic toy data only, so they do not bear on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue, from theory plus experiments, that hierarchical latent structure in the data is a major driver of the Hydra effect, induction heads and function vectors. They call hierarchy necessary, given that gradient decorrelation and readout concavity are present but not sufficient. They say the resulting redundancy makes ablation-based interpretability and alignment hard.
record.recipe_differences: Uses layer-output ablation and downstream predictive-influence measurements, but applies them in controlled synthetic training regimes and limits the large-model measurement to the immediately following layer.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect depends on data-generation structure: hierarchical toy and PCSG settings show compensation, while flat toy and N-gram settings show near-zero or no emergence. In the toy comparison the layerwise signal is weaker than the headwise signal. In the large-model experiments, compensation is described as deeper-layer activity early in training and middle-layer-localized after training.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, headwise zero ablation produces downstream compensation in target-token logit contribution under hierarchical data but near zero under flat data (d=1.82, p<0.001).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head-level compensation depends on hierarchical latent structure in the training data.

record.problems: The toy layerwise result is weak and does not survive Bonferroni correction. Large-model layerwise ablation is restricted to the immediately following layer. Most plotted values are not stated numerically in the text. The toy experiments use 10 independent seeds; headwise evidence is from synthetic data rather than general text.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying layerwise compensation results were left out. Headwise results are included as rows r8–r9 but linked to none of the listed versions because the measure is not full-distribution compensation on general text.

untested.parts: How much of the output is restored. Layer pairs other than adjacent ones in the large-model runs. Ablation of attention sublayers alone.
Not tested: no late-MLP erasure measurement.
Not tested on general text or across families and sizes; the headwise results are toy synthetic only.
Not tested: no per-prompt variance or overcorrection reported.
Not tested: copy suppression, LayerNorm and anti-erasure are only cited.
Not tested: only zero ablation is used.
Only discussed (intervention-based interpretability is 'extremely challenging'); not measured.

missing.what: Layerwise Hydra effect sizes and p-values for the toy hierarchical-versus-flat comparison (final, peak, AUC windows)

record.verdict_notes: The study's definition ∆(l)=⟨WU[xt],h(l)⟩ makes it unclear whether h(l) is a layer's output or the residual stream; this affects how the Hydra score reads. No final LayerNorm is included in ∆(l). The large-model results are figure-only with no stated numbers or uncertainty. The record's limits_scope label on early-training rows was dropped, because a shift in where compensation occurs does not qualify V1.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test all layer pairs in the large-model experiments; there it measures only the effect on the immediately following layer. It does not establish restoration of the full output distribution.
Late-MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token and its change under earlier ablations are not measured.

The headwise experiment is on controlled synthetic data and measures a correct-token predictive-influence score, not self-repair on the full distribution across general text, model families, and sizes.
The study does not report prompt-level variation or overcorrection relative to the original effect.
It does not test backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons as mechanisms of the measured compensation.
The reported ablations zero layer or head outputs; mean and resample ablations are not tested.
The study discusses consequences for intervention-based interpretability but does not measure whether ablation-based importance scores misstate component contributions.

rows.subject: Transformer trained on hierarchical DGP (toy model; model name not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed an upstream layer's residual contribution and measured downstream target-token predictive influence.
rows.measure: Layerwise Hydra score: downstream change in target-token predictive influence after upstream layer ablation.
rows.baseline: Unablated predictive influence, as used in the Hydra-score comparison.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this individual value; the layerwise hierarchical-versus-flat signal had one-sided p < 0.05 but did not survive Bonferroni correction.
rows.note: The authors describe the layerwise signal as weaker than the headwise signal and attribute this partly to ablations removing multiple heads whose effects can cancel.
rows.check: State is right: the signal is weak (one-sided p<0.05, not surviving Bonferroni). The ablation zeroes a whole layer's residual contribution, not only the attention sublayer named in V1, and the measure is a raw change in downstream logit contribution, not the fraction of output restored.

rows.operation_detail: Zeroed an upstream layer's residual contribution and measured downstream target-token predictive influence.
rows.measure: Layerwise Hydra score: downstream change in target-token predictive influence after upstream layer ablation.
rows.baseline: Unablated predictive influence, as used in the Hydra-score comparison.
rows.value: figure only; described as near-zero relative to the hierarchical condition
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this individual value
rows.note: The paper reports the flat counterpart as near zero; the paired hierarchical-versus-flat layerwise result did not survive Bonferroni correction.
rows.check: The 'near-zero counterparts' wording in Sec 4.3 refers to the headwise, induction and FV metrics. For the flat model the text says only 'no sign of Hydra effect'. No layerwise flat value is stated; it is figure only.

source_check.correct: No numerical layerwise value is stated. Section 4.3 reports no sign of Hydra effect in the flat variant; its near-zero description concerns headwise Hydra, induction and function-vector metrics.
source_check.problem: The near-zero description is assigned to the wrong metric.

rows.subject: Transformer trained on hierarchical DGP (toy model; model name not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed an attention head's value output before the output projection and measured downstream predictive influence.
rows.measure: Headwise Hydra score: maximum downstream change in target-token predictive influence.
rows.baseline: Unablated predictive influence, as used in the headwise Hydra-score comparison.
rows.value: figure only; the headwise score is reported as substantially higher than for the flat DGP
rows.uncertainty: At final evaluation, paired effect size d = 1.82 for the hierarchical-versus-flat headwise comparison; p < 0.001 across reported aggregation windows and tests, surviving Bonferroni correction.
rows.note: This is a controlled synthetic-data headwise result and a target-token predictive-influence measure, not a full-distribution result on general text.
rows.check: Headwise compensation in a 6-layer toy on synthetic data. This is not general text or multiple families as V3 requires. The hierarchical model shows a clear effect (d=1.82 versus flat), so the state is observed rather than partial.

tranche.reason: The study addresses downstream compensation, but zeroes whole-layer residual contributions rather than resampling attention sublayers. Its large-model measure is restricted to the next layer's predictive influence, and it does not quantify restored output.

source_check.notes: Substantive methods and results were readable; fragmented Figure 2 checkpoint labels prevent confident verification of the approximately 739k endpoint. Toy-model p-values and d=1.82 concern hierarchical-versus-flat comparisons, not the fraction of output restored.
